sections.label: Content note
sections.body: **Content note:** this page discusses the abuse of older people, disabled people and children, and deaths in nursing homes. [Where to report abuse is listed below.](#kop-ri-report)

sections.label: Not the troubled teen industry
sections.heading: Not the troubled teen industry
sections.body:
Nursing homes are not part of the troubled teen industry, and Kids Over Profits does not track nursing homes or assisted living facilities.

They hold the same kind of people teen programs do, and that is what makes both dangerous. Older people, disabled people and children depend on others for their care, cannot leave, and are the people least likely to be believed. The two grew out of the same institution, and today some of the same investors own both and run them the same way: every bed filled, as few staff as they can manage.

We are not experts on long-term care. Residents, their families, ombudsmen and the organizations listed below have done this work for decades.

sections.label: Cut off and not believed
sections.heading: Cut off and not believed
sections.body:
Abuse happens where the victim depends on the abuser and cannot tell anyone, and that describes older people, disabled people and children alike. Older people are most at risk when they "depend on others for help with activities of everyday life," have "disabilities, memory problems, or dementia," or have no family or friends nearby, and many are too ashamed or afraid to report it.[^1] Disabled children are abused for the same reasons: the World Health Organization names stigma, placement in institutions, and communication impairments that leave children "hampered in their ability to disclose abusive experiences."[^3] In a facility, the person they depend on is the staff, and the staff admit it: in nursing homes and long-term care facilities, 2 in 3 staff say they committed abuse in the past year.[^5]

Table: What the studies counted
| Who | What was found | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Disabled children | 3.4 times as likely to be maltreated as other children | [^2] |
| Disabled people 12 and older | Victims of violent crime at almost 4 times the rate of others | [^4] |
| Former teen program residents, surveyed for Congress in 2007 | 93 percent had their mail monitored, 96 percent their calls | [^6] |

Children in teen programs are vulnerable for the same reasons, and the programs cut them off further. They kept residents from home, read their mail, listened to their calls and told parents in advance not to believe their children: "They told us he would lie to us about what was going on at the school to manipulate us; they told us to ignore his letters. We were not allowed to talk to him on the phone," one parent said.[^6] Bob Bacon, whose son Aaron died in a Utah wilderness program in 1994, told the same hearing that the program's "policy had predetermined that these kids are all liars and manipulators and, therefore, Aaron was faking."[^6] Seventeen years later the Senate Finance Committee found residential treatment facilities doing the same: they "often cut off a child from their communities by limiting communication with families/guardians."[^7]

> Their policy had predetermined that these kids are all liars and manipulators and, therefore, Aaron was faking.
> -- Bob Bacon, whose son died in a Utah wilderness program, to Congress in 2007

sections.label: Once in the same buildings
sections.heading: Once in the same buildings
sections.body: They were once held in the same buildings. For centuries elderly, sick and disabled people and poor children were put in the same workhouses and almshouses ([orphan care timeline](/orphanages/)). In the United States, Dorothea Dix investigated almshouses and jails from 1841 into the 1880s and found children, elderly people and people with mental illness confined together, the children neglected, unschooled and exposed to physical and sexual abuse. Reformers moved the children out: New York's Children's Law of 1875 barred children aged 3 to 16 from county poorhouses, and disabled children went to institutions of their own, one of the roots of the troubled teen industry ([how the threads met](/birth-of-the-tti/)). The old and disabled people stayed in the poorhouses.

sections.label: The same owners, the same business
sections.heading: The same owners, the same business
sections.body:
The same investors have owned both, and they run both by cutting the people who watch over the residents.

Table: Investors that have owned nursing homes and youth programs
| Investor | Nursing homes | Youth programs |
|---|---|---|
| The Carlyle Group | HCR ManorCare, one of the largest chains, from 2007 until it went bankrupt in 2018 owing $7.1 billion[^8][^9][^10] | Newport Academy, by 2017; sold to Onex in 2021[^11][^12] |
| Onex | Skilled Healthcare Group, 70 nursing and assisted living homes in California, Texas, Nevada and Kansas, bought in 2005 and merged into Genesis HealthCare in 2015[^13][^14] | ResCare (a stake in 2004, the rest in 2010): residential treatment, group homes and foster care for "young people with emotional and behavioral issues" and "juveniles in the justice system," renamed BrightSpring Health in 2018[^15][^16][^17]; a majority of Newport Healthcare from 2021[^12] |

Two West Virginia programs under the ResCare name are in our records.

What that ownership does to nursing homes has been measured. A study of Medicare patients found that a private equity buyout raised a nursing home's patient mortality by about 11 percent; nurse staffing fell after the buyouts, which the authors name as one reason for the deaths.[^18] Private equity owners of care providers make each facility a separate legal entity, which limits the investors' liability, and load the companies with debt to pay shareholders, which pushes facilities to cut staff ([corporatization timeline](/corporatization/)).

Youth program owners say the same thing out loud. Jay Ripley, who co-founded [Sequel Youth and Family Services](/operator/sequel-tsi/), told business students in 2015, "You can make money in this business if you control staffing." In 2024 the Senate Finance Committee quoted him to conclude that understaffing is "a cornerstone of the RTF business model",[^20] and found youth residential treatment filling beds while cutting staff ([our summary](/warehouses-of-neglect/)).[^19]

For these investors a nursing home bed and a youth program bed are the same product: filled by someone who cannot leave and will not be believed, and made to pay by cutting the staff who would see what happens to them.

If you know of another investor that has owned both nursing homes and youth programs, please [tell us](/contact/).

sections.label: Where to report abuse
sections.heading: Where to report abuse
sections.body:
- **If someone is in danger now**, call 911.
- **Long-Term Care Ombudsman.** Every state has one. Ombudsmen take complaints from nursing home and assisted living residents and their families, and work for the resident. Find yours through the Eldercare Locator, 1-800-677-1116, or [Consumer Voice's directory](https://theconsumervoice.org/get-help/).
- **State survey agency.** Complaints about abuse, neglect, too few staff or unsafe conditions in a nursing home go to the state survey agency, usually part of the state health department. CMS lists [each state's agency](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/health-safety-standards/quality-safety-oversight-general-information/contact-information), or call 1-800-MEDICARE, 1-800-633-4227 (TTY 1-877-486-2048), for the contact.
- **Adult Protective Services** takes reports of abuse, neglect and exploitation of older and disabled adults. Find your state's number through [NAPSA](https://www.napsa-now.org/help-in-your-area/).
- **Medicaid Fraud Control Units** investigate and prosecute [abuse and neglect of residents](https://oig.hhs.gov/fraud/medicaid-fraud-control-units-mfcu/) in facilities that take Medicaid.
- **Protection and Advocacy.** For disabled residents, including younger people who want to leave a nursing home, there is a [Protection and Advocacy agency](https://www.ndrn.org/about/ndrn-member-agencies/) in every state and territory.
- **988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline**, 24 hours: call or text [988](tel:988).

For abuse in a youth program, see [our reporting directory](/report-abuse/).

sections.label: Organizations to learn from
sections.heading: Learn from the people who work on this
sections.body:
- [National Consumer Voice for Quality Long-Term Care](https://theconsumervoice.org/): Founded in 1975 as the National Citizens' Coalition for Nursing Home Reform; speaks for long-term care residents nationally and runs the National Long-Term Care Ombudsman Resource Center.
- [Long Term Care Community Coalition (nursinghome411)](https://nursinghome411.org/): Publishes nursing home staffing, inspection and antipsychotic data and guides for residents and families.
- [Center for Medicare Advocacy](https://medicareadvocacy.org/): A nonprofit law organization; tracks nursing home enforcement and residents' rights.
- [Justice in Aging](https://justiceinaging.org/): Legal advocacy for older adults with low incomes, including the rights of people living in nursing homes.
- [California Advocates for Nursing Home Reform](https://canhr.org/): Fact sheets, legal referrals and advocacy for people in California's long-term care facilities.
- [ADAPT](https://adapt.org/): A disability rights group, led by disabled people, that fights for the right to live at home instead of in nursing homes.

sections.label: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.heading: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.body: If you live or work in long-term care, or have a family member who does, and something here is wrong or missing, please [tell us](/contact/). We will correct it.
